title: What's the Deal with Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain condition caused by repeated blows to the head, long known as punch drunk syndrome or dementia pugilistica in boxers. They cover Dr. Harrison Martland's early description, Dr. Bennett Omalu's 2002 diagnosis of Mike Webster as the first NFL player with CTE, the NFL's response and disability committee, the risks for children and youth football, subconcussive impacts, the three symptom stages, the tau-protein mechanism and postmortem-only diagnosis, UCLA imaging research on living patients, NFL concussion numbers, the NFL's funding controversy and settlement, and the documentary League of Denial. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about violence against women in horror films.

entities.name: Journal of the American Medical Association

segments.title: Opening and introduction to CTE
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, noting the movie Concussion and recommending the Frontline documentary League of Denial based on the Fainaru brothers' book. They name the condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) and mention earlier episodes on concussions.

segments.title: Early history: punch drunk and boxers
segments.summary: Dr. Harrison Martland described punch drunk symptoms in boxers in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The hosts explain CTE looks like Parkinson's and dementia under a microscope but comes from repeated head blows, and discuss boxing and calls to ban it since the 1950s.

segments.title: Mike Webster and the first NFL diagnosis
segments.summary: Bennett Omalu examined the brain of Pittsburgh Steelers center Mike Webster, who died of a heart attack at age fifty. He found tau proteins but not beta amyloid, and diagnosed CTE, the first NFL player diagnosed with it.

segments.title: NFL response, disability claim, and Omalu's public controversy
segments.summary: The hosts describe the NFL's long downplaying of concussions and its disability committee ruling for Webster's family. They also discuss Omalu's public statements, including his comment about O.J. Simpson, and the work of Ann McKee.

segments.title: Risks for children and youth football
segments.summary: The hosts discuss research suggesting children are at higher risk because of undeveloped neck muscles and myelin, with Robert Cantu cited. They note girls may be more susceptible and that risk extends to other sports and activities such as soccer heading, hockey, rugby, and car crashes.

segments.title: Subconcussive hits and symptoms by stage
segments.summary: The hosts explain subconcussive impacts that cause no visible symptoms but accumulate, then describe three stages of CTE symptoms, from dizziness, headaches and impulse control problems to memory loss, slowed movement, and speech difficulty. They note the link to aggression and depression is not yet conclusively established.

segments.title: Tau protein mechanism and diagnosis
segments.summary: CTE can only be diagnosed after death. The hosts explain how tau proteins stabilize microtubules in neurons, become hyperphosphorylated and accumulate, killing neurons and leading to region-level brain death. They note the mechanism is not fully understood.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the discussion of prevention and the NFL.

segments.title: Prevention, NFL concussion numbers, and research funding controversy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the lack of a cure and the difficulty of avoiding head hits in football. They cite NFL concussion counts from 2014 and 2015 and PBS Frontline's tracking, rule changes such as kickoff moves, and a congressional report about the NFL's $30 million NIH gift and the later withdrawn funds. They describe the NFL acknowledging the CTE link in March and a settlement with former players.

segments.title: CTE in former players and UCLA brain imaging research
segments.summary: The hosts cite a study of 165 former football players, 131 of whom had CTE, and discuss donation bias. They describe UCLA researchers using MRI brain volume shrinkage to explore possible live diagnosis. They also cite Alzheimer's rates among former NFL players and the depression and suicide findings, which they question.

segments.title: League of Denial, Junior Seau, and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts recommend League of Denial, describe the NFL's efforts to suppress awareness, and discuss the competing researchers and the situation around Junior Seau's brain after his death. They close by suggesting listeners search for CTE on the site.

segments.title: Listener mail: violence against women in horror
segments.summary: A listener named James responds to a previous episode about horror stories and violence against women, arguing that horror reflects real-world violence against women. The hosts agree it is a good point and thank him. Hosts give contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact details and sign off.
